newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand business weeklies - Oct 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand business weeklies - Oct 25.

text.p: THE NATIONAL BUSINESS REVIEW

Reserve Bank governor Don Brash appears to be losing the fight with foreign investors over interest rates. High real rates have attracted so much international capital that interest rates are actually being pushed down. The Reserve Bank indicated on Thursday that monetary conditions had become a little firmer than desired.
Cavill White Securities managing director Don Turkington believes the Reserve Bank will have to allow the 90-day rate to ease by mid-December, probably below nine percent. Page 1

The Dairy Board could be in the market to buy a leading international food brand or brands to expand its consumer product business. The board, New Zealand's biggest single exporter, would need foreign equity partners to make the purchases. The board is floating the idea to test dairy farmer support for a move that would consolidate its transition from a commodity supplier to a major global food company and position it to challenge multinational giants Nestle and Kraft. Page 1.

Tradenz chief executive Rick Christie is coy about his new job after his surprise resignation at Tuesday's board meeting. The former BP oilman and Cable Price Downer managing director said only that he was reutring to the private sector, taking a senior management position in Wellington. An announcement is expected next week. Page 1.

Investment Savings and Insurance Association, a newly-established industry lobby, is pushing to get taxation of investment gains put on the agenda for the secret coalition government talks. It is concerned about a creeping de facto
capital gains regime and believes this does not encourage retirement savers to consider the full range of investment options open to them. Page 2.

The 22-year-old Tasman crewing accord has collapsed, with the prospect of foreign ships having unlimited access to the already highly competitive Tasman trade. While cracks had been weakening the accord for some time, the end came with the surprise announcement last month of a deal struck between the Maritime Union of Australia and BHP Transport. The MUA has allowed BHP to operate nine of its foreign-crewed ships to carry
cargo in competition with the dedicated New Zealand and Australian Tasman fleets, to accusations of betrayal from New Zealand unions. Page 6.

TVNZ does not want to sell its 16.3 percent stake in Sky but is said to be happy with the bid by News Corporation-controlled Independent Newspapers (INL) to take a major holding in the leading pay-TV operator. Others appear less than thrilled and another legal scrap over Sky-buy places is on the wind, NBR reports. Earlier this year, Telecom shelved a proposal to buy 25 percent of Sky after a protracted court battle with Clear and
BellSouth and objections from cable-TV operator Saturn. Page 11.

New Zealand First supporters overwhelmingly prefer a coalition deal with Labour rather than National, according to the latest NBR-Consultus poll carried out last Friday and at the weekend. Some 63 percent of New Zealand First voters favoured a coalition with Labour against 22 percent wanting to link up with National. Seven percent wanted neither. Of all those surveyed, 45 percent favoured a New Zealand First-Labour link, against 37 percent support for a New Zealand First National deal. Seven percent favoured neither arrangement. Page 14.
THE INDEPENDENT

New Zealand stocks soared, interest rates eased and the New Zealand dollar slid back one cent against the greenback on Thursday following a signal from the Reserve Bank it considered monetary conditions a tad tight. Essentially, monetary conditions should be eased from too tight to tight in line with guidlines officially set out in September, the statement from David Archer, Reserve Bank's financial markets department chief manager said. Page 1.

The bottom has fallen out of the Australian ostrich market leaving Kiwi punters an estimated $200 to $300 million out of pocket. According to a recent Sydney Morning Herald article disenchanted Australian investors are dumping entire ostrich flocks onto the market, sending prices into a nose dive. Page 1.

Independent Newspapers Ltd's bid to buy into Sky Network Television will, if successful, plug New Zealand into Rupert Murdoch's global pay television network, giving the media magnate control of both our biggest newspaper publisher and pay-tv operator. The key issue for the Commerce Commission, the
Commerce Ministry and Sky's rival is what - if any - programming agreements would be attached to the sale. Whoever can access the best programmes wins the viewers and their money. Page 3.

European shipping firm Interkarel is preparing to take the Ministry of Fisheries to court to challenge what it regards as the illegal seizure by fisheries inspectors of five of its vessels. The firm is also finalising legal action which could make New Zealand the first country to be hauled before a just-established international tribunal in Hamburg for allegedly breaching the International Law of Sea Convention, Interkarel's
lawyer Hakan Schiller said. Page 6.
